title: Digital public infrastructure can expand fiscal capacity and social assistance, but only when inclusion, trust, and institutional reach travel with it
source_unit: IMF Note 2026/009, Digitalization for Stronger Revenue and Social Assistance in the Middle East and Central Asia
geography: Middle East and Central Asia comparative evidence, with country cases across Gulf Cooperation Council, Caucasus and Central Asia, non-GCC Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan

denominator.unit: Middle East and Central Asia comparative digitalization assessment

digital_tools.value: tax e-services, e-filing, e-payments, e-invoicing, third-party data exchange, AI-based risk audits, digital payment tracking, and dynamic social registries

fiscal_route.value: digital tools improve information, streamline procedures, strengthen enforcement, and can raise revenue and fiscal transparency

readiness_bottlenecks.value: infrastructure, skills, financial inclusion, public-sector capacity, legal frameworks, governance, and trust constrain reach

distributional_risk.value: digital exclusion, data-security threats, system disruption, and higher enforcement or compliance costs can accompany expansion

observations.method: IMF comparative synthesis of digital-readiness indicators, revenue-administration evidence, social-assistance measures, selected country cases, and related empirical correlations.
observations.uncertainty: The note combines cross-country indicators, case studies, and associations; it does not establish one universal causal effect of digitalization or identical results across countries and groups.
observations.subgroup: Taxpayers, benefit recipients, women and rural residents with lower financial inclusion, public officials, firms, informal workers, and people exposed to digital or administrative exclusion.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital tools may improve traceability and targeting while increasing surveillance, error, or enforcement burdens; stronger administrative data does not by itself mean fairer policy or better treatment.

observations.period: 2021 or latest available; digital access and inclusion comparison

denominator.unit: regional and peer comparison of national ID, financial account, mobile phone, and internet access measures

access_pattern.value: national ID and mobile access are relatively widespread across much of the region, while financial inclusion and internet access remain more uneven, particularly among women and rural populations

readiness_gap.value: Gulf Cooperation Council and many Caucasus and Central Asia countries are more advanced, while fragile, conflict-affected, and low-income settings face larger infrastructure, skills, capacity, legal, and trust gaps

reach_condition.value: digital ID, connectivity, financial accounts, and payment rails must connect for digital public finance to reach people in practice

observations.method: IMF use of World Bank ID4D and Global Findex measures, IMF AI preparedness and GovTech indicators, and regional comparisons; the latest year varies by indicator.
observations.uncertainty: The indicators are not a contemporaneous household service-outcome panel and may lag rapidly changing digital conditions; access does not measure usability, consent, error correction, or actual benefit receipt.
observations.subgroup: Women, rural households, financially excluded people, residents of fragile or conflict-affected settings, people without reliable connectivity, and people dependent on public transfers.
observations.counterinterpretation: High mobile or ID coverage can coexist with weak affordability, limited autonomy, poor service quality, or exclusion from accounts and payments; low adoption may sometimes reflect reasonable privacy or safety preferences.

registry_route.value: broader, dynamic, and interoperable social registries are associated with more efficient spending

outcome_route.value: social assistance is more effective at reducing poverty and inequality where government digitalization and financial inclusion are stronger

core_operations.value: identification, verification, and payment systems are minimum operational levers through which digital tools can improve targeting and delivery

coordination.value: the largest gains arise when digital reforms are coordinated across fiscal functions and supported by digital ID, interoperable systems, and digital payments

observations.method: IMF synthesis of social-safety-net indicators, social-registry comparisons, digitalization measures, simulated poverty and inequality effects, and country cases.
observations.uncertainty: Reported relationships do not prove that digitalization alone caused better poverty or inequality outcomes; targeting accuracy, benefit adequacy, political choices, administrative discretion, and program design remain consequential.
observations.subgroup: People in poverty, households with unstable income, women, rural residents, people lacking accounts or documentation, and officials responsible for eligibility, payments, and appeals.
observations.counterinterpretation: More interoperable registries can improve reach but can also magnify data errors, exclusion, privacy loss, or automated denial unless people can correct records and contest decisions.

boundary: This record adds a digital-public-infrastructure route linking identity, connectivity, financial inclusion, interoperable registries, tax administration, revenue, social-assistance targeting, poverty, inequality, trust, exclusion, privacy, and enforcement costs. It is not a country-level causal evaluation, a guarantee that digitization improves equity, a measure of individual benefit receipt, or evidence that digital systems can substitute for adequate benefits, accountable institutions, or human remedy.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official IMF Note 2026/009 PDF reviewed for its abstract, digital-readiness constraints, revenue and social-assistance mechanisms, access indicators, registry/payment coordination, and distributional risks.
